The reactive core: a fine-grained signal graph with named state, incremental collections and
live text. Design: `docs/design/reactive-core.md`.

The reactive graph (design: `docs/research/reactive-design-v2.md`).

Layers and their contexts:
- inputs: signals and named state, written only from handlers and `watch` callbacks;
- derive: `memo`, pure, tracked, may not write;
- observe: property bindings, structural regions and `watch` sources, tracked, may not write;
- effects: handlers and `watch` callbacks, untracked, may write.

Algorithm: push marking (Dirty on direct observers, Check further down), pull evaluation, memo
early cutoff, bindings before watches, creation order. A node is marked Clean *before* it runs,
so a re-mark during its own run (a watch writing its source) schedules another run.

Invariants: no runtime borrow is held while user code runs or while a value is dropped (values
may own other nodes, e.g. a list owns its item signals); handles carry generations.
A derived value: lazy, recomputed when its inputs change, propagated only when it changes.

Incremental collections (design §3; DBSP / ILC): a `List` and composable views over it.

Every collection is a *stage*: an ordered set of keys with an item per key, a bounded log of
structural changes (`Insert` / `Remove` / `Move`, each with the index at that moment) and
observers that receive value-level events (`inserted`, `removed`, `updated(old, new)`,
`moved`). A view is an observer of its upstream stage and a stage itself, so views compose:
`list.filter(..).sort_by(..)`, `list.group_by(..)` with per-group members.

Each stage keeps its order in a `Seq` (order-statistic treap), so every event costs
O(log n) (O(log² n) where a rank among members is needed). The UI layer renders a stage by
applying its log (`Source::subscribe` / `Source::take`); a `Move` moves a row.

virtualization) with subtree sums, so `prefix_weight(i)` and `index_at_weight(y)` are O(log n):
the "sum tree" GPUI and Rune use for long lists. The reference implementation is a `Vec`; the
tests compare the two on random operations.

Async work owned by scopes: tasks, timers on the app's clock, channels from other threads,
background work, and resources (keyed async loads with their state as signals).

- A task (`spawn`) belongs to the scope it was spawned in and is dropped (cancelled) when the
  scope is disposed; `detach` lets one outlive its scope. Tasks run on the UI thread, like
  handlers: they may write signals.
- Every result from another thread comes back one way: it wakes a task, which the runtime
  polls at a frame boundary. Woken tasks run in spawn order, so the order threads finish in
  does not change what happens.
- Time is the app's clock (`App::advance`), never the wall clock: `sleep`, `interval` and
  `now` follow it, so tests decide when timers fire.
- Pending work is listed (`App::pending`), with the scope and source location of each.

items.sig: pub fn virtual_each<K, T>(source: impl Fn() -> Source<K, T> + 'static, estimate: impl Fn(&T) -> f32 + 'static, row: impl Fn(&K, ReadSignal<T>) -> View + 'static) -> View where K: Eq + Hash + Clone + Display + 'static, T: Clone + 'static
items.docs:
Like [`each`], for long lists: only rows near the visible area exist. Put it directly in a
scroll container (`v_flex().overflow_y_scroll().flex_1()`); it follows that container's
scroll offset and height.

Row heights start from `estimate` and are replaced by each row's measured height once it
has been laid out; the first visible row stays put while rows above it are measured
(scroll anchoring). Rows are kept in a weighted order-statistic tree, so offset → row and
row → offset are O(log n) and an update costs O(visible · log n) whatever the length. The
two spacers are `{parent id}-top` / `-bottom`.

The GPU renderer: wgpu, one WGSL shader (`shader.wgsl`), one instance per display-list item,
one draw call per frame. Glyphs and paths are rasterized as by the reference renderer
([`GlyphCache`], [`paths`]) and packed into an alpha atlas (masks; a path larger than a tile
takes several) and an RGBA atlas (color glyphs). When an atlas fills up, every atlas starts
over and the frame is built again with only what it draws.

Path rasterization, shared by both renderers: strokes become outlines (kurbo), and a path's
coverage is computed on the CPU by zeno into an 8-bit mask, which the reference renderer blends directly and the GPU renderer
samples from its mask atlas. Both therefore draw the same coverage.

A mask is keyed by the path's content, the transform's linear part, the translation's
subpixel phase (quarter pixels, as glyphs), the style and the visible region: a path that
only moves by whole pixels reuses its mask, and a path larger than what is visible is
rasterized only where it shows.

Fonts for deterministic tests and screenshots: the core bundles only Latin faces (Inter, IBM
Plex Mono), and windows use the platform's fonts, so text in other scripts renders as
missing glyphs headless. A test registers these instead of relying on the machine's fonts:

```
let mut app = octara::app::App::new(|| octara::view::text("你好").into());
octara_fonts::cjk::install(&mut app);
```

They are a dev-dependency, not part of an app.
